examples: She *can* memorize twenty words in one day. (present ability)
Last year he *couldn't* pass the exam. (past, negative)
Next June she will *be able to* graduate from college. (future ability)
I have *been able to* concentrate better since I found a quiet library. (present perfect)
He *was able to* win a scholarship after months of hard study. (past, formal)
grammar.explanation:
Use **can** for present ability or possibility. She **can** memorize twenty new words in one day.

For past ability, use **could**. Last year I **couldn't** pass the exam, but now I **can**.

**Can** has no future or perfect form. For those tenses, use **be able to** + verb. Next June she will **be able to** graduate from college.

Use **be able to** after "have" too. She has **been able to** concentrate better since she changed her study habits.

**Be able to** also works in the present and past when you want to sound more formal. "I **was able to** finish the assignment" sounds more careful than "I **could** finish it."

Past negative: **couldn't** and **wasn't able to** mean the same. He **couldn't** get the scholarship last year.

Quick recap: **can** = now. **could** = past. **be able to** = every other tense.
